rationale: B wins because it gives the founder cleaner, more pitchable desks and harder proof gates, especially in "An unprofitable automaker turns its charging network into a revenue line." A has useful bones, but "Rivian just became a charging-network operator. Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet" invents a market reaction it cannot know. B's weakest line, "the connector fight is over," is still an overreach, but the set mostly catches its own risk and asks for the right evidence before anyone embarrasses themselves.
gaps_in_A: "Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet" is invented. No stock move, analyst note, or valuation evidence appears in the update.

"After Tesla, Rivian opens its charging network to all EVs. The proprietary-charger era is fading" leans on external Tesla/category context the prompt did not give and turns one Rivian announcement into an industry thesis.
Angle 1 and angle 4 overlap more than they admit: both are basically Rivian monetizing chargers while unprofitable, just aimed at different business desks.
"move the needle" appears in the proof section. It is on the blacklist, and it is exactly the kind of lazy phrase this exercise is supposed to punish.
gaps_in_B: "Every new Rivian stall will carry both plugs — the connector fight is over" overclaims from one Rivian fact. Dual connectors at new stalls do not end a standards fight by themselves.
"joining the small set of automaker-owned networks" is plausible but not supplied in the update; either source it or strip it.

"it is competing for the same drivers rather than negotiating with their manufacturers" stretches "no partnership announced" into a strategy claim. B correctly asks for confirmation, but the angle still leads too hard.
"If you want to strengthen the standards angle" in the next step is minor fluff. The right instruction is simply to find a current CCS/NACS peg or kill that angle.
